sources.title: Éric Gourgoulhon, An Introduction to Relativistic Hydrodynamics, arXiv:gr-qc/0603009v1
sources.locator: Full 37-page PDF; §4.3, equations (4.10)–(4.14) (PDF pp. 15–16), and §§5.2–5.3, equations (5.4)–(5.9) (PDF pp. 17–18): equation-of-state and first-law conventions, perfect-stress divergence, and its energy projection.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete §4.3 equation-of-state and first-law discussion, equations (4.10)–(4.14), including the independent state variables and thermodynamic derivative conventions.
source_review.supports: The distinction between a supplied relativistic-fluid state function and its temperature/chemical-potential derivatives, and the local thermodynamic conventions used for comparison.
source_review.limitations: The notes use a particle-number state and do not supply the entropy-only map or its inverse. The item defines its own positive-temperature functions and does not import a particle current, quantum coefficient, or empirical equation of state.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete perfect-fluid calculation in §5.2, equation (5.4), including the stress divergence and its decomposition into energy and momentum terms.
source_review.supports: The perfect-fluid stress form and its covariant divergence, used as an independent comparison for the local tensor expansion.
source_review.limitations: The source includes its own multicomponent thermodynamics and conserved-number currents. The item derives the entropy-current identity directly from the defined entropy-only state map without assuming those currents.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete parallel-projection calculation in §5.3, equations (5.5)–(5.9), including the energy equation and multicomponent first-law substitution.
source_review.supports: The energy projection of stress-energy conservation and its first-law substitution, used as an independent comparison for the entropy-current argument.
source_review.limitations: The source includes its own multicomponent thermodynamics and conserved-number currents. The item derives the entropy-current identity directly from the defined entropy-only state map without assuming those currents.

scope_checks.reason: The selected equation-of-state and perfect-fluid conservation sections do not treat the fixed-rest Cattaneo thermal subsystem or its quadratic Lyapunov identity.

sources.title: Nicolas Borghini, Elements of Hydrodynamics, University of Bielefeld lecture notes (2022)
sources.locator: Full 202-page PDF; Chapter X.3.1–X.3.2 (PDF pp. 157–160) and Chapter XI.2.1 (PDF pp. 177–178): perfect-fluid stress and entropy calculation, radiation equation-of-state comparison, and temperature scaling.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete X.3.1 discussion of the charge four-current and perfect-fluid energy-momentum tensor, including the comoving charge and energy-density definitions.
source_review.supports: The notes define comoving energy density and pressure and the perfect-fluid stress form, giving context for the scalar state quantities used locally.
source_review.limitations: This section uses conserved-charge fluid variables and does not supply the entropy-only state chart; the item defines its own maps and makes no quantum or empirical coefficient claim.

contents.name: X.3.1 Charge four-current and energy-momentum tensor of a perfect fluid

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete entropy-conservation proof in Chapter X.3.2 a, equations (X.22) and the displayed derivation through the normalized-velocity contraction.
source_review.supports: An independent perfect-fluid entropy-current argument for comparison with the local energy-projection proof.
source_review.limitations: The source uses Gibbs–Duhem and conserved charge currents in its general entropy proof. The submitted proof derives the entropy-current divergence directly from its entropy-only state map without assuming those currents.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete zero-charge temperature-scaling calculation in Chapter XI.2.1, including equations (XI.17)–(XI.19) and the Gibbs–Duhem and fundamental-relation substitutions.
source_review.supports: For an ideal ultrarelativistic gas without conserved charge, the notes give p=ε/3 and derive ε proportional to T^4 and s proportional to T^3.
source_review.limitations: The derivation establishes proportionality and does not determine the positive coefficient a_R; the item treats it as a parameter and proves map identities by direct calculus.

scope_checks.reason: The selected perfect-fluid entropy and Bjorken-flow sections do not present the fixed-rest Cattaneo system or its quadratic entropy and Lyapunov identities.

sources.title: N. Andersson and G. L. Comer, Variational multifluid dynamics and causal heat conductivity, arXiv:0908.1707v1
sources.locator: Full 15-page PDF; §4, “The extended thermodynamics view,” equations (4.2)–(4.12) (PDF pp. 5–7), especially the rigid-solid linearization and constant-parameter Cattaneo reduction.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete displayed rigid-solid branch from its simplified momentum equation through the linearized near-equilibrium equation and equations (4.9)–(4.12).
source_review.supports: The constant-parameter Cattaneo constitutive equation as a linear near-equilibrium heat-conduction model, and the distinction from the zero-relaxation Fourier limit.
source_review.limitations: This variational multifluid derivation does not prove global solutions, a quadratic Lyapunov estimate, finite propagation for every datum, or a relativistic speed bound. Those are proved conditionally and algebraically in the item.

scope_checks.reason: The selected rigid-solid heat-conduction section does not treat radiation thermodynamic state maps.
The selected rigid-solid heat-conduction section does not establish an entropy-only perfect-fluid state identity.

sources.title: N. Andersson and G. L. Comer, Heat conduction in rotating relativistic stars, arXiv:1804.01520v1
sources.locator: Full 13-page PDF; §2.1, equations (1)–(3) and surrounding discussion (PDF pp. 1–2), comparing Fourier diffusion, the Cattaneo equation, and the telegrapher equation.

source_review.read_extent: Read the complete §2.1 discussion from the energy equation and Fourier law through the Cattaneo law and its telegrapher-equation consequence.
source_review.supports: A second treatment of the finite-relaxation thermal model and its phenomenological status in a relativistic setting.
source_review.limitations: The paper does not establish the speed inequality or the PDE energy argument. Its reported motivation and physical discussion are not used as empirical premises.
